Part 1

Why logistic regression?

What it is, why linear regression falls short, and the maths behind the fix

Part 1 · What is logistic regression?

What is logistic regression?

  • Logistic regression model (also known as logit model) is often used for classification and predictive analytics
  • Often, the output variable we want to predict is not continuous, so we can’t use linear regression. e.g. Class section A/B, Pass/Fail, Yes/No, 0 or 1, True/False, etc.
  • Sometimes, we want to predict the probability of some event z, i.e. the probability of the instance being that class.
  • i.e. learn p(z∣x)
  • Since the output is a continuous probability, the output variable needs to be bounded between 0 and 1.

Part 1 · Why not linear regression?

The problem with using linear regression for our question today

Remember linear regression? It predicts continuous outcomes (like shoe size):

y^​=β0​+β1​x1​+β2​x2​+...+βp​xp​

where y^​ is the predicted value (any real number, −∞ to +∞), β0​ the intercept, βi​ the coefficients and xi​ the predictors (like height in cm).

But our question has a binary outcome

Section A, or section B (not A). We can still ask for the probability of A, which is continuous. But remember, linear regression can give you values below 0 (negative probabilities?) and above 1 (probabilities > 100%?).

Part 1 · Why not linear regression?

What happens if we try using linear regression?

Code

# Create a binary outcome from section: A -> 1, B -> 0
# (C and 'Prefer not to say' become NaN, so those rows are left out)
df['section_bin'] = df['section'].map({'A': 1, 'B': 0})

# Try linear regression (the WRONG way)
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

model = smf.ols('section_bin ~ height_cm', data=df).fit()
print(model.summary())

Part 1 · Why not linear regression? · ISLR §4.2

Why not just turn the categories into numbers?

A patient arrives at the emergency room with symptoms that could come from one of three conditions: stroke, drug overdose or epileptic seizure. We could code the diagnosis as a number Y and fit least squares…

  • Coding 1 quietly claims an order (overdose sits between stroke and seizure) and equal gaps (stroke → overdose is the same distance as overdose → seizure). There is no reason this needs to be true.
  • Coding 2 is just as reasonable, but implies a totally different relationship. Each coding produces a fundamentally different linear model, and different predictions for new patients.
  • A 1, 2, 3 coding only makes sense if the categories have a natural order with similar gaps, e.g. mild, moderate, severe. In general there is no natural way to turn a qualitative response with more than two levels into a number.

Coding 1

YDiagnosis
1stroke
2drug overdose
3epileptic seizure

Coding 2

YDiagnosis
1epileptic seizure
2stroke
3drug overdose

Problem (a)

A regression method cannot accommodate a qualitative response with more than two classes.

ISLR §4.2 Why Not Linear Regression?

Part 1 · Why not linear regression? · ISLR §4.2–4.3

Two classes: closer, but still not a probability

  • With two classes, a 0/1 dummy works (0 = section B, 1 = section A): fit least squares and predict class 1 when Y^>0.5. Flipping the coding gives the same predictions.
  • Y^ is even a crude estimate of Pr(Y=1∣X), but nothing keeps it between 0 and 1. On ISLR’s credit-card Default data, the line predicts a negative probability of default for balances near zero.
  • Any straight line fit to a 0/1 response predicts p(X)<0 for some X and p(X)>1 for others, unless the range of X is limited.

Problem (b)

Even with just two classes, a regression method will not provide meaningful estimates of Pr(Y∣X).

We need something better: logistic regression (§4.3)

Don’t model Y directly. Model the probability that Y belongs to a category, e.g. Pr(default=Yes∣balance), with a function whose output is always between 0 and 1. Then classify with a threshold: p>0.5, or lower (say 0.1) if a bank wants to be cautious.

Why not linear regression? Quick check

Think (or talk to your neighbour) first, then open each answer.

Q1Which of these outcomes needs logistic rather than linear regression: (a) a student’s shoe size, (b) whether a student is in section A, (c) a student’s travel time to HKU?Answer

(b). Section A / not A is a binary outcome. Shoe size and travel time are continuous, so linear regression suits them.

Q2Our OLS fit was section_bin​=0.3909+0.0007×height. At what height does this “probability” of being in section A go above 1?Answer

Set 0.3909+0.0007h=1: h=(1−0.3909)/0.0007≈ 870 cm. (It would only drop below 0 at a negative height, about −560 cm.) Nobody is that tall, but nothing in a straight line stops it. Our line is almost flat because height barely predicts section; with a stronger predictor it would pass 0 or 1 within real heights. A logistic model never can.

Q3What are some reasons not to use a regression method for a qualitative response?Answer

(a) It can’t accommodate a qualitative response with more than two classes. (b) Even with two classes, it won’t give meaningful estimates of Pr(Y∣X): some estimates fall outside [0, 1].

Part 2

The mathematics of logistic regression

Part 2 · The maths

Building intuition: odds

  • Linear regression’s prediction y^​ can be any number. For a logistic model, we need to transform it in a way that will bound it between 0 and 1. How can we do this?
  • A first step: take the odds of the event
Odds=P(event does not occur)P(event occurs)​=1−pp​

Example 1

If P(morning lark) = 0.75

Then P(night owl) = 0.25

Odds = 0.75 / 0.25 = 3

Interpretation: A student who did this survey has odds of 3 of being a morning lark.

Example 2

If P(section A) = 0.5

Then P(section B) = 0.5

Odds = 0.5 / 0.5 = 1

Interpretation: A student has the same, equal odds (1) of being assigned to section A or B.

Part 2 · The maths

From probability to odds

Probability (p)Odds (p/(1−p))Interpretation
0.100.1111:9 against
0.250.3331:3 against
0.501.000Even odds
0.753.0003:1 in favor
0.909.0009:1 in favor

But there’s still a problem…

  • If we set the odds equal to the line, 1−pp​=β0​+β1​x, the right-hand side can go below 0, but odds can never be negative.
  • Odds are lopsided: p from 0 to 0.5 gives odds 0 to 1, but p from 0.5 to 1 gives odds 1 to +∞ (see the table).
  • We want a scale that, like the straight line, takes any value from −∞ to +∞ and spreads the output evenly. Now what should we do?

Check your understanding · 2

Odds Quick check

Think (or talk to your neighbour) first, then open each answer.

Q1If P(night owl) = 0.8, what are the odds of being a night owl? And of being a morning lark?Answer

Night owl: 0.8 / 0.2 = 4 (4:1 in favour). Morning lark: 0.2 / 0.8 = 0.25 (1:4).

Q2What probability corresponds to odds of exactly 1?Answer

p = 0.5: the event is as likely to happen as not (“even odds”).

Q3Why isn’t “odds = β0​+β1​x” good enough yet?Answer

Odds can only be 0 to +∞, and lopsided: p from 0–0.5 is squeezed into 0–1, while p from 0.5–1 is stretched over 1–∞. A straight line can still go negative, which odds never can.

Part 2 · The maths

Solution: the log-odds (logit)

We can take the natural logarithm of odds:

Log-Odds=ln(1−pp​)=logit(p)

We can also write the function as

logit(p)=β0​+β1​x

where logit(p) is the log-odds (logarithm of odds) of the event.

Note

Mathematically, the logit is the inverse of the standard logistic function σ(x)=1+e−x1​.

Why logarithm?

Odds: 0 to +∞ (still problematic)

Log-odds: −∞ to +∞ (perfect for linear modeling!)

Part 2 · The maths

A quick reminder: logarithms

Note

The logarithm (or “log” for short) is the power to which you have to raise the base to obtain a given number. You have to raise 10 to the power 4 to produce 10,000, so log10​(10,000) = 4.

The “natural” logarithm is when you use the constant e (≈ 2.718) as a base. e (Euler’s number) is a common and useful math constant (like π).

Part 2 · The maths

The logistic regression equation

The core equation: after 2 transformations, we get:

ln(1−pp​)=β0​+β1​x1​
  • Left side = log-odds of the outcome
  • Right side = linear combination of predictors (just like linear regression!)
  • p = probability of outcome occurring
  • βi​ = coefficients (log-odds change per unit increase in xi​)

Converting back to probability: since we want a probability, solve for p:

p=1+eβ0​+β1​x1​eβ0​+β1​x1​​

or more directly:

p=1+e−(β0​+β1​x1​)1​

This is called the logistic function or sigmoid function!

Check your understanding · 3

Log-odds Quick check

Think (or talk to your neighbour) first, then open each answer.

Q1What range can the log-odds take, and why does that make it a good partner for β0​+β1​x?Answer

−∞ to +∞, exactly the range of a straight line. The line can take any value and still correspond to a valid probability.

Q2If p=0.5, what are the log-odds? What does a positive log-odds tell you?Answer

ln(0.5/0.5)=ln(1)= 0. Positive log-odds mean p>0.5; negative log-odds mean p<0.5.

Q3In ln(1−pp​)=β0​+β1​x1​, what does β1​ tell you directly?Answer

The change in the log-odds of the outcome for a one-unit increase in x1​. It is not the change in probability.

Part 2 · The maths

The sigmoid function

p(x)=1+e−x1​
  1. Always between 0 and 1: no matter what the linear combination equals!
  2. S-shaped curve: smooth transition from 0 to 1
  3. Symmetric around 0.5: when linear part = 0, probability = 0.5
  4. Interpretable coefficients: related to odds ratios

Code

x = np.linspace(-10, 10, 200)
y = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(x, y, linewidth=3, color='darkblue')
plt.axhline(y=0.5, color='red', linestyle='--', alpha=0.5, label='p=0.5 (decision boundary)')
plt.axvline(x=0, color='gray', linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)
plt.xlabel('Linear Combination (when beta_0 = 0, beta_1 = 1)', fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel('Probability', fontsize=12)
plt.title('The Sigmoid Function: Converting Linear to Probability', fontsize=14)
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.legend()
plt.ylim(-0.1, 1.1)
plt.show()

Output

Part 2 · Summary

Summary: linear vs. logistic regression

The transformation chain:

  1. Start: Linear combination → β0​+β1​x1​+...+βp​xp​ (range: −∞ to +∞)
  2. Transform to odds: Odds=eβ0​+β1​x1​+...+βp​xp​ (range: 0 to +∞)
  3. Transform to probability: p=1+OddsOdds​ (range: 0 to 1)
  • Linear regression uses a straight line. Logistic regression passes that line through the logistic function (S-shaped curve), so its output can’t go below 0% or above 100%.
  • The coefficients are read differently too: as changes in log-odds or odds, not in the outcome itself (Part 3).

Rule of thumb

If you’re trying to predict “how much” of something that is continuous (e.g., weight in kg), you’d typically use linear regression. If you’re trying to predict the probability of whether something will happen or the probability of what category something belongs to (e.g., class section), logistic regression is usually the better choice.

Check your understanding · 4

The sigmoid Quick check

Think (or talk to your neighbour) first, then open each answer.

Q1What probability does the sigmoid give when β0​+β1​x=0? What about a very large positive, or very large negative, value?Answer

At 0: 1+e01​=21​= 0.5. Very large positive: e−x→0, so p→1. Very large negative: e−x is huge, so p→0. It gets close to 0 and 1 but never reaches them.

Q2Put these in order, from model to answer: probability, linear combination, odds.Answer

Linear combination (−∞ to +∞) → odds =elinear (0 to +∞) → probability =1+oddsodds​ (0 to 1).

Q3Linear or logistic? (a) Predicting weight in kg from height. (b) Predicting whether a student plays an instrument from their age.Answer

(a) Linear: “how much” of a continuous quantity. (b) Logistic: the probability of a yes/no outcome.

Part 3 · Interpreting coefficients

Interpreting coefficients: three ways

For each coefficient β there are 3 ways to interpret it: 1. log-odds (direct), 2. odds ratio (exponentiate), 3. probability (plug into the logistic function).

  1. Log-odds interpretation (direct)
    • One unit increase in x results in a change (increase if +, decrease if −) in log-odds of the y variable
    • For our example, a 1cm increase in height will result in a 0.0028 increase in the log-odds of being in section A (holding all else constant)
    • which is a 0.0028 increase in ln(p(class_section=B)p(class_section=A)​)
    • which takes the log-odds from 0.0392 to 0.0392 + 0.0028 = 0.0420. Check: e0.0420≈1.0429, the new odds on the next slide.
    • hard to understand intuitively

For our example

Intercept coefficient = −0.4371

height_cm coefficient = 0.0028

Odds of being in Class A is: 1.0400

Log-odds of being in Class A is: 0.0392 (= ln 1.0400)

These are the odds for the whole class (52 of the 102 students in section A or B are in A). In the fitted model they belong to a student about 170 cm tall, so read these steps as starting from a typical student.

Part 3 · Interpreting coefficients

2. Odds ratio interpretation (exponentiate)

  • If we exponentiate, one unit increase in x multiplies the odds by eβ1​, i.e. it changes (p(class_section=B)p(class_section=A)​). The change is multiplicative.
  • For our example: e0.0028 ≈ 1.0028, the “odds ratio”. The odds of being in section A go from 1.0400 to 1.0400 × 1.0028 ≈ 1.0429, which is higher than before.
  • But how much higher? (1.0429 − 1.0400) / 1.0400 ≈ 0.0028, so a 1cm increase in height results in a ≈ 0.28% increase in the odds of being in section A.
  • For a 2cm increase, multiply by 1.0028 twice: 1.0400 × 1.0028 × 1.0028. Q: How would that affect the odds of being in section A?

Caution

This is NOT the same as saying a 1cm increase in height will result in a 0.28% increase in the probability of being in class A

Code

import numpy as np 
print(np.exp(0.0028)) # To calculate what is e^0.0028
print(f"New odds: {1.0400 * 1.0028:.4f}")
print(f"Difference between new and original odds: {(1.0429-1.0400):.4f}")
print(f"Proportion of difference in odds to original odds: {(0.0029 / 1.0400):.4f}")

Output

1.0028039236612292
New odds: 1.0429
Difference between new and original odds: 0.0029
Proportion of difference in odds to original odds: 0.0028

Why is it called the “odds ratio”?

The odds ratio is literally the ratio of two odds under different conditions: Odds Ratio = Oddsheight​Oddsheight+1cm​​. When we say “multiply the odds by 1.0028,” that multiplication factor IS the odds ratio: it’s the same number expressed as either a multiplier or as a ratio comparing new odds to old odds.

Check your understanding · 6

Log-odds and odds ratios Quick check

Think (or talk to your neighbour) first, then open each answer.

Q1The height coefficient is 0.0028. In one sentence, what does it mean on the log-odds scale?Answer

Each extra cm of height raises the log-odds of being in section A by 0.0028, holding everything else constant.

Q2How would a 2 cm increase in height affect the odds of being in section A?Answer

Multiply by the odds ratio twice: 1.00282=e0.0056≈1.0056. So the odds rise by about 0.56%. The changes multiply rather than add, although with an effect this small the result is almost exactly 2 × 0.28%.

Q3True or false: “a 0.28% increase in the odds” means “a 0.28% increase in the probability”.Answer

False. Odds and probability are different scales. How much the probability changes depends on where you start, which is what the next slides show.

Part 3 · Interpreting coefficients

3. Probability interpretation

  • Most easy to understand intuitively, but hardest to calculate and requires careful interpretation
  • Unlike log-odds and odds ratio interpretations (which have constant effects), the probability change from a 1cm height increase depends on the baseline probability level
  • You can still ask “What does a 1cm increase in height do to the probability of being in section A, holding all else constant?” BUT the answer depends on what baseline values you start from
    • The change in effect on probability is largest when the baseline probability is around 0.5, and gets smaller as the probability approaches 0 or 1
  • Recall the logistic function: p=1+e−(β0​+β1​×height_cm)1​

Try it

Given the coefficient estimates from our example, can you calculate the probability of being in section A given that a student is 165cm tall?

Part 3 · Interpreting coefficients

Calculating with Python

p=1+e−(β0​+β1​⋅height_cm)1​

Code

import math

# Given coefficients
intercept = -0.4371
height_coef = 0.0028

# Student height
height_cm = 165

# Calculate linear combination (log-odds)
log_odds = intercept + height_coef * height_cm
print(f"Log-odds (at height = 165cm): {log_odds:.4f}")

# Calculate probability using logistic function
probability = 1 / (1 + math.exp(-log_odds))
print(f"Probability of being in section A: {probability:.4f}")
print(f"Probability as percentage: {probability * 100:.2f}%")

Output

Log-odds (at height = 165cm): 0.0249
Probability of being in section A: 0.5062
Probability as percentage: 50.62%
  • What does this probability mean?
  • What do you think should happen if we put in different heights?
Example interpretation at a specific baseline
  • At 165cm height: probability of section A = 50.62%
  • At 166cm height: probability of section A = 50.69%
  • The 1cm increase raises probability by 50.69 − 50.62 (≈ 0.07) percentage points at this baseline
  • If we started from a different baseline (say 90% probability), the same 1cm increase would produce a much smaller change in probability: about 0.03 percentage points instead of 0.07

Check your understanding · 7

Probabilities Quick check

Think (or talk to your neighbour) first, then open each answer.

Q1Using β0​=−0.4371 and β1​=0.0028, what is the probability of being in section A for a 175 cm student?Answer

Log-odds =−0.4371+0.0028×175=0.0529. Then p=1+e−0.05291​≈ 0.513 (51.3%). Taller than 165 cm, so higher than 50.6%.

Q2Why can’t we say “each extra cm raises the probability of section A by 0.07 percentage points”?Answer

Because the S-curve isn’t a straight line. 0.07 points is the change at 165 cm, where p≈0.5 and the curve is steepest. Near p=0.1 or 0.9, the same 1 cm changes p much less.

Q3Which interpretations give the same answer whatever the starting height?Answer

Log-odds (always add β1​) and odds ratio (always multiply by eβ1​). Only the probability change depends on the baseline.

Part 4

Logistic regression for classification

From probabilities to class labels, and how to judge a classifier

Part 4 · Classification

Classification vs. regression

  • We’ve now seen multiple different types of regressions in class
    1. Linear regression, continuous input and output (e.g., height → shoe size)
    2. Linear regression with at least one categorical input (e.g., gender + height → shoe size)
    3. Logistic regression, continuous input and a probability as output (e.g., height → probability of class section)
  • Notice how the output of these models are all continuous values? What if you wanted to predict something that was categorical or discrete?

Regression models

Predict a continuous output variable (e.g., shoe size, height, weight). Evaluated with metrics like mean squared error or R-squared.

Classification models

Predict a categorical or discrete output variable (e.g., class section, favourite season, gender). Evaluated with metrics like accuracy or precision/recall.

The goal for classification

Assign a class/category label to previously unseen data points as accurately as possible. Despite its name, logistic regression adapts the linear regression framework to do exactly this.

Part 4 · Classification

How to do classification

  • Given a series of input/output pairs (x(i),y(i)), we represent each observation x(i) by a feature vector [x1​,x2​,…,xn​] and compute an output: a predicted class y^​(i)∈{0,1}
  • For each feature (i.e. input variable) xi​, weight wi​ tells us the importance of xi​. We sum up the weighted features and a bias term b into a score z, then classify based on the threshold r:
z=w⊤x+by={10​ if z≥r if z<r​​
z=(i=1∑n​wi​xi​)+b
  • Think of it like a voting system where each feature gets a vote weighted by its importance. If the total “votes” exceed the threshold, predict y=1 (“yes”); otherwise y=0 (“no”).

The x variables (features/inputs)

The measurable characteristics of whatever you want to classify (like age, height, or gender).

The w variables (weights/parameters)

Learned during training, like the beta coefficients in regression. Positive: higher values push toward class 1. Negative: toward class 0. Large magnitude: strong influence; small: weak.

The bias b

A baseline adjustment: it shifts the score up or down regardless of the input features, which moves the decision boundary/threshold.

Tip

This simple approach forms the foundation for more complex algorithms like neural networks, transformers, and “AI”.

Check your understanding · 8

Classification basics Quick check

Think (or talk to your neighbour) first, then open each answer.

Q1Regression or classification? (a) Predicting favourite season. (b) Predicting height. (c) Predicting whether a bank transaction is fraudulent.Answer

(a) Classification: a category. (b) Regression: continuous. (c) Classification: fraud / not fraud, one of ISLR’s examples.

Q2A feature has a large, negative weight wi​. What does that tell you?Answer

Higher values of that feature push the prediction strongly toward class 0. The sign gives the direction; the size gives the strength of the influence.

Q3What job does the bias term b do?Answer

It’s a baseline adjustment: it moves the score z up or down regardless of the inputs, which shifts where the decision threshold falls.

Part 4 · Classification

Logistic regression for classification

  • We’d like a principled classifier that gives us a probability: p(y=1∣x) and p(y=0∣x). So we need to formalize “sum is high”.
  • However, z=w⊤x+b isn’t a probability, it’s just a number!
  • Solution: the sigmoid function from Part 2 maps any number to a probability between 0 and 1:
p=σ(z)=1+e−z1​
  • So we pass the score through the sigmoid and treat the result as a probability:
P(y=1)P(y=0)​=σ(w⋅x+b)=1+e−(w⋅x+b)1​=1−σ(w⋅x+b)​

Part 4 · Classification

From probability to class: the decision boundary

Then, to turn the probability into a classifier:

y^​={10​if p(y=1∣x)>0.5, i.e. if w⋅x+b>0otherwise​

Here, 0.5 is the decision threshold. The inputs where p(y=1∣x)=0.5 form the decision boundary.

Part 4 · Classification

Where did the w’s come from?

  • Supervised classification:
    • We know the correct label y (either 0 or 1) for each x.
    • But what the system produces is an estimate, y^​.
  • We want to set w and b to minimize the distance between our estimate y^​ and the true y.
  • We need a distance estimator: a loss function or a cost function (similar to what ordinary least squares does for linear regression)

A loss function

Cross-entropy loss

An optimization algorithm

Stochastic gradient descent: updates w and b to minimize the loss (or cost)

In the software we used

Minimising cross-entropy is the same as maximum likelihood (“Method: MLE” in the statsmodels output). statsmodels finds the answer with Newton’s method; scikit-learn’s LogisticRegression uses L-BFGS and, by default, adds a small penalty on large weights (C=1.0), so its coefficients can differ slightly from statsmodels’.

Why not least squares? A straight line fitted to 0/1 labels predicts values below 0 and above 1, as we saw in Part 1. We could fit the S-curve itself by (non-linear) least squares, but maximum likelihood is preferred because it has better statistical properties (ISLR §4.3.2).

Check your understanding · 9

From probability to class Quick check

Think (or talk to your neighbour) first, then open each answer.

Q1For one student, z=w⋅x+b=1.5. What is P(y=1), and which class does the model predict?Answer

σ(1.5)=1+e−1.51​≈ 0.82. That’s above 0.5, so the model predicts class 1.

Q2Why is the rule “p>0.5” the same as the rule “w⋅x+b>0”?Answer

The sigmoid equals exactly 0.5 at z=0 and only ever increases with z. So p>0.5 happens exactly when z>0.

Q3Linear regression picks its coefficients by least squares. How does logistic regression choose w and b?Answer

By minimising a loss function (cross-entropy loss) with an optimisation algorithm such as (stochastic) gradient descent. The Method: MLE line in the statsmodels output is the same idea: maximising the likelihood is equivalent to minimising cross-entropy.

Part 4 · Class example

Why split data? Train/test sets

Splitting our data helps prevent overfitting and provides unbiased evaluation:

  • In machine learning, it’s essential to have separate data for training our model and testing its predictions. This helps us evaluate the model’s performance on unseen data and gives us an idea of how it might perform in real-world scenarios.

Training set (60–70%)

  • Used to fit model parameters (w, b)
  • Model learns patterns from this data
  • e.g., think of sample test questions, or questions in class slides

Test set (15–30%)

  • We test our model on this data
  • Never used during training
  • Provides unbiased estimate of final performance
  • Simulates real-world deployment
  • e.g., exam questions
  • Typical proportion of train/test set is 0.7/0.3 (without a validation set)

Note

Sometimes, we also need an additional split of the data called the Validation set (but we will not need it for now)

Check your understanding · 10

Setting up a classifier Quick check

Think (or talk to your neighbour) first, then open each answer.

Q1Only 14% of the class are morning larks. How often would a “model” that always says night owl be right?Answer

About 86% of the time (137 of 160). That’s the baseline a useful classifier has to beat, so a high accuracy on its own can be misleading.

Q2Why do we judge the model on a test set it never saw during training?Answer

To get an unbiased estimate of how it will do on new, real-world data. Scoring it on its own training data rewards memorising (overfitting), like marking students on the exact questions they practised.

Q3Next we split the data with test_size=0.3. How many of our 160 students end up in the test set, and how many in training?Answer

48 in the test set and 112 in training: 0.3 × 160 = 48. That 48 is the “support” total (42 + 6) you’ll see in the classification report.

Part 4 · Class example

Logistic regression classification

  • Can age help us predict whether you are a morning lark or a night owl?

Code

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression #Another way to do Logistic Regression
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, roc_auc_score, roc_curve

# Create features (X) and target (y) for our model
X = df[['age']]  # Features: just age column, keep as DataFrame
y = df['chronotype_bin']  # Target: binary outcome (0=night owl, 1=morning lark)

# Split data into training and testing sets
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=2025)

# Create and train the logistic regression model
model = LogisticRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)

# Make predictions on test set
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
y_pred_proba = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]  # Probability of being a morning lark

# Evaluate model performance
print("Classification Report:")
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred))
print(f"\nROC AUC Score: {roc_auc_score(y_test, y_pred_proba):.3f}")

weighted avg       0.77      0.88      0.82        48

Part 4 · Evaluating a classifier

Classifier evaluation metrics

Confusion Matrix:

(TNFN​FPTP​)

Key Metrics:

  • Accuracy: TP+TN+FP+FNTP+TN​
  • Precision: TP+FPTP​ (positive predictive value)
  • Sensitivity/Recall: TP+FNTP​ (true positive rate)
  • Specificity: TN+FPTN​ (true negative rate)
  • F1-Score: Precision+Recall2×Precision×Recall​

Part 4 · Evaluating a classifier

Five metrics from the confusion matrix

Here, TP = true positives, TN = true negatives, FP = false positives, and FN = false negatives — the four cells of the confusion matrix on the previous slide. Each metric is a different ratio of those cells.

MetricQuestion it answersBenefitLimitation
AccuracyTP+TN+FP+FNTP+TN​ What share of all predictions were correct? It is a simple, intuitive summary of overall performance, and it works well when classes are fairly balanced and both error types matter about equally. It can be misleading with imbalanced data. If only 1% of emails are spam, a model that never flags spam is still 99% accurate.
Precisionpositive predictive valueTP+FPTP​ When the model predicts positive, how often is it right? It shows how trustworthy positive predictions are, which helps when false positives are costly. For example, a spam filter shouldn’t send important emails to the junk folder. It ignores missed positives. A model can achieve high precision by flagging only its most obvious cases.
Sensitivity / recalltrue positive rateTP+FNTP​ Of all actual positives, how many did the model find? It shows how well the model avoids missing positives, which helps when false negatives are costly, such as in cancer screening or fraud detection. It ignores false alarms. A model that labels everything positive achieves 100% recall.
Specificitytrue negative rateTN+FPTN​ Of all actual negatives, how many did the model correctly rule out? It shows how well the model avoids false alarms among negative cases. This helps when wrongly flagging them is harmful, such as confirmatory medical testing that could lead to unnecessary treatment. It also complements sensitivity by showing performance on the negative class. It can look strong when negatives vastly outnumber positives, even if many of the model’s positive predictions are wrong. It also says nothing about how many positives were found.
F1-scoreharmonic mean of precision and recallPrecision+Recall2×Precision×Recall​ How well does the model balance precision and recall? It combines both into one number and is high only when both are high, because the harmonic mean penalizes a large gap between them. This makes it useful for imbalanced data and for comparing models. It ignores true negatives and weights precision and recall equally, even when one type of error is more costly.

Part 4 · Evaluating a classifier

ROC curve and AUC

ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) Curve:

  • Plots True Positive Rate vs False Positive Rate
  • Shows trade-off between sensitivity and specificity
  • AUC (Area Under Curve): Single metric summarizing ROC
    • AUC = 0.5: Random classifier
    • AUC = 1.0: Perfect classifier
    • AUC > 0.8: Generally considered good

Mathematical definition

TPR = TP+FNTP​ (Sensitivity)

FPR = FP+TNFP​ (1 − Specificity)

Part 4 · Evaluating a classifier

ROC curve for our logistic regression

  • ROC AUC Score: 0.587
  • Good or bad?

Check your understanding · 11

Judging a classifier Quick check

Think (or talk to your neighbour) first, then open each answer.

Q1Our confusion matrix is [[42, 0], [6, 0]]. Work out the accuracy and the recall for morning larks.Answer

Accuracy =4842+0​= 0.875 (0.88 in the report). Recall (morning larks) =TP+FNTP​=0+60​= 0. The accuracy looks high only because 42 of the 48 test students are night owls: the model called every test student a night owl, so it never found a single morning lark.

Q2Our AUC is 0.587. Good or bad?Answer

Only a little better than random guessing (0.5), and far below the 0.8 rule of thumb. Age on its own hardly separates morning larks from night owls, and with only 48 test students (just 6 of them morning larks) the estimate is noisy too.

Q3ISLR notes that a credit card company might flag customers when p>0.1 instead of p>0.5. Why?Answer

To be conservative: a lower threshold catches more of the people who really will default (higher recall/sensitivity), at the cost of more false alarms (lower specificity). The threshold is a choice that depends on which mistake is more costly.

Summary

  • Understand the fundamental concepts of logistic regression.
  • Comprehend the sigmoid function and its role in logistic regression.

Looking ahead

Beyond logistic regression

How today’s model connects to support vector machines, decision trees and neural networks

Looking ahead · 1/3 · Support vector machines

Logistic regression → support vector machines

  • Same shape of model. Both compute a score z=w⋅x+b and split the classes where z=0: a straight line (a hyperplane with more features). Both are linear classifiers.
  • Different way of choosing w and b. Logistic regression minimises cross-entropy, so every point nudges the line a little. An SVM looks for the line with the widest margin; only the points on or inside the margin, the support vectors, decide where it goes.
  • Different output. Logistic regression gives a probability, σ(z). An SVM gives a class: which side of the line. Getting probabilities from an SVM needs an extra step, Platt scaling, which is a logistic regression fitted to the SVM’s scores.
  • Curved boundaries. With the kernel trick, an SVM can draw curved boundaries without you creating new features by hand.
For the curious: the two loss functions

Code the classes as y=±1 and let z=w⋅x+b.

Logistic regression (cross-entropy): log(1+e−yz). Never exactly zero, so every point counts.

SVM (hinge loss): max(0, 1−yz). Exactly zero once a point is safely past the margin, so those points don’t matter.

The two curves have very similar shapes, which is why the two models often give similar answers (ISLR §9.5).

Looking ahead · 2/3 · Decision trees

Logistic regression → decision trees

A different family of model, but closely connected.

  • How it decides. No weighted sum: a tree asks yes/no questions about one feature at a time (“Is x2​>4.0?”). Its boundary is made of axis-aligned steps, so it can capture “x2​ high and x1​ low”, which one straight line can’t (95% vs 87% training accuracy here).
  • Probabilities too. A tree’s probability is the share of each class in the leaf a point lands in: coarse steps instead of a smooth S-curve.
  • Same yardstick. With criterion="entropy", a tree picks the split that most reduces the same cross-entropy that logistic regression minimises (scikit-learn also calls it "log_loss").
  • Boosted trees borrow the logistic link. Gradient boosting (e.g. XGBoost, GradientBoostingClassifier) adds up many small trees to predict the log-odds, then applies the sigmoid: logistic regression with trees in place of the straight line.

The tree as rules (export_text)

|--- x2 <= 4.0
|   |--- class: 0
|--- x2 >  4.0
|   |--- x1 <= 5.4
|   |   |--- class: 1
|   |--- x1 >  5.4
|   |   |--- class: 0

Looking ahead · 3/3 · Neural networks

Logistic regression → neural networks

  • One neuron = logistic regression. A neuron takes a weighted sum z=w⋅x+b and passes it through an activation function. With a sigmoid activation and cross-entropy loss, a single neuron is logistic regression.
  • Same training recipe. Cross-entropy loss, minimised by (stochastic) gradient descent, as on “Where did the w’s come from?”. Backpropagation is how a network works out the gradient for every weight.
  • A network stacks neurons in layers. Hidden layers turn the inputs into new, learned features (usually with a ReLU activation rather than the sigmoid). For a yes/no output, the last neuron is a logistic regression on those features; with more than two classes it becomes softmax, the multi-class version of logistic regression.
  • That’s why the tip earlier called this the foundation for neural networks, transformers and “AI”.

Looking ahead · Summary

Four classifiers at a glance

Logistic regressionSVMDecision treeNeural network
How it decidesweighted sum → sigmoidweighted sum → which side of the linea chain of yes/no questionslayers of weighted sums + activations
Boundarystraight linestraight line with the widest margin; curved with kernelsaxis-aligned stepsany shape it can learn
Probabilities?yes, smoothnot directly (Platt scaling)yes, coarse (leaf shares)yes (sigmoid / softmax output)
Trained withcross-entropy (maximum likelihood)hinge loss + widest margingreedy splits (Gini or entropy)cross-entropy + gradient descent
Easy to explain?yes: odds ratioslinear: fairly; kernel: hardyes: if/else rules (small trees)hard
Reach for it when…you want probabilities and effects you can explain; a good first baselinemany features; classes fairly well separatedinteractions, mixed feature types; forests/boosting for accuracylots of data: images, text, audio

Further reading: ISLR Ch. 8 (tree-based methods), §9.5 (relationship between SVMs and logistic regression), Ch. 10 (deep learning).

Check your understanding · 12

Beyond logistic regression Quick check

Think (or talk to your neighbour) first, then open each answer.

Q1A single neuron with a sigmoid activation is trained by minimising cross-entropy. Which model from today is that?Answer

Logistic regression. Its weights and bias play the roles of β1​,…,βp​ and β0​, and its output σ(w⋅x+b) is p.

Q2Logistic regression and a linear SVM both draw a straight line. How do they choose it differently, and what does each give you?Answer

Logistic regression minimises cross-entropy using every point and gives a probability. An SVM finds the widest margin, set only by the support vectors, and gives a class; for probabilities it needs Platt scaling, which is a logistic regression on its scores.

Q3In the tree example, class 1 lives where x2​>4 and x1​≤5.4. Why does a depth-2 tree beat logistic regression there, and how could you help logistic regression?Answer

The tree carves out the corner with two yes/no splits. Logistic regression on x1​ and x2​ alone can only draw one straight line. Giving it extra features, such as an interaction term or yes/no indicator features like “x2​>4”, lets it bend.
